item.title: U.S. launches strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in Strait of Hormuz
item.description:
What to know about the Iran war today: The U.S. launched strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, according to an Iranian official. The strikes came hours after Iran said it targeted a U.S. radar system in Bahrain. U.S. Central Command said those attack drones were all intercepted. Iran also claimed Tuesday that another oil tanker was on fire near the Strait of Hormuz after striking a sea mine. Daily claims by the regime of ships hitting mines have not been confirmed, and the U.S. military says the shipping lanes in the southern strait are mine-free and safe to use.Vice President JD Vance told Fox News on Monday that the Trump administration won't let the Iran war become a two-year commitment, but he reiterated the White House's justification for launching the war, insisting that Iran's nuclear program remains a threat to the United States.
New Updates
6:59 PM / November 17, 2026
Kuwait military says it's facing "hostile drone attacks"
Kuwait's military on Tuesday said it was hitting back at "hostile drone attacks," urging the public to follow security and safety advice.
"The General Staff of the Army notes that any explosion sounds heard are the result of air defense systems intercepting hostile attacks," the Kuwaiti army wrote on X. No other details were provided, and no one has claimed responsibility for the attack.
Kuwait is among U.S. allies in the Middle East that have faced attacks from Iran since the start of the war.
Earlier Tuesday, Bahrain said its air defense systems had successfully intercepted Iranian drones as Iran claimed to have struck a U.S. radar system in the kingdom.

item.title: Man with ax destroys $60M U.S. military plane, prosecutors say
item.description:
An ax-wielding man breached a security perimeter and destroyed an American military plane while it was parked overnight at an Irish airport, cutting hydraulic lines, smashing cockpit gauges and pouring ball bearings into fuel tanks, U.S. prosecutors said. The man's supporters attributed the attack to his anger at the United States' involvement in Middle East conflicts.
An indictment unsealed Tuesday in Manhattan charges Daithi O'Corrain, 48, with destruction of U.S. government property in connection with the April incident at Shannon Airport, an international gateway in the west of Ireland that serves as a hub for American troops and military equipment.
O'Corrain isn't in U.S. custody and his arraignment on the new charge hasn't been scheduled. If convicted, he faces up to 10 years in prison. Online court records do not list an attorney who might speak on his behalf.
The plane, a $60 million U.S. Air National Guard C-130 Hercules that had been en route to a military assignment in another country, was rendered inoperable and won't fly again, U.S. prosecutors said. The attack jeopardized critical military operations, the FBI said.
O'Corrain, described by supporters as an independent peace activist, was arrested immediately after the attack by Ireland's police force, An Garda Síochána. He was charged there with causing criminal damage and trespassing. The Limerick Post reported he is from Cork, about 60 miles southeast of Shannon.
Manhattan U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said the indictment sends "a clear and powerful message that attacks on U.S. military assets — and thus our national security — will not be tolerated."
An online fundraiser organized by people describing themselves as O'Corrain's friends and comrades said he disarmed the C-130 in protest of the U.S.'s war with Iran and support for Israel's war in Gaza — a flashpoint in Ireland, where many people have expressed solidarity with Palestinians.

item.title: American soldier accused of spying in U.S. custody after U.K. arrest
item.description:
A United States Army soldier arrested in the United Kingdom on suspicion that he engaged in espionage linked to Russia has been taken into the custody of the U.S. military, British and American officials said Tuesday.
A U.S. official previously identified the suspect as Lt. Col. Brandon Tyner, a senior human resources officer based at Imjin Barracks, home to the headquarters of NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps. Tyner, 41, joined the Army in 2008 and has been deployed to Afghanistan, Qatar and Iraq.
Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing, said in a news release that U.S. authorities will continue the investigation. The suspect is expected to be charged soon.
"These are extremely serious allegations, and our collective response should send a strong message that we will act swiftly and robustly where we suspect this kind of espionage activity taking place," Taylor said.
The soldier is suspected of violating the U.K.'s National Security Act of 2023 to obtain or disclose protected information and to assist a foreign intelligence service. The London Metropolitan Police said the suspected activity relates to Russia. Federal Bureau of Investigation director Kash Patel said that the soldier was "a potential threat to national security."
He was arrested by the the London Metropolitan Police during a sting operation in Gloucester, about 100 miles west of London, on November 10. The operation involved the Met Police's Counter Terrorism Policing Unit, the U.S. military and the FBI.
"This FBI has zero tolerance for anyone who betrays their oath to the United States or puts our national security at risk," FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement on Tuesday.
Officials have carried out further searches in Gloucestershire, the county where Gloucester is located, related to the investigation, the Metropolitan Police Department said.

item.title: U.S. identifies remains of 6 soldiers killed in Korean War, including teens
item.description:
Six soldiers who died in the Korean War, including two teenagers, have been accounted for decades after their deaths, the Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency announced Monday.
The identifications are part of an ongoing effort to locate and identify the remains of those killed in the Korean War. When a soldier is marked as accounted for, they receive a burial with full military honors.
U.S. Army Cpl. Jackie Lee Thurman was a member of Battery B, 99th Field Artillery Battalion, 1st Cavalry Division. Thurman, 18, was a forward observer near Waegwan, South Korea, when his post came under heavy attack, according to the agency, and was last seen trying to evacuate a shell-shocked officer from the area while under heavy enemy fire.
Afterward, Thurman was reported missing in action. A presumptive finding of death was issued on Dec. 31, 1953. His remains were declared unrecoverable two years later, in January 1956.
The agency said that a set of remains, designated X-5814 Tanggok, was recovered by the Quartermaster Graves Registration Company near Kumhwa-dong, South Korea, in October 1952. The remains were interred as unknowns at the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific in Honolulu, Hawaii. In November 2022, the agency disinterred the remains. Analysis allowed the agency's scientists to identify the remains as Thurman's. He was marked as accounted for by the agency on May 18, 2026.

item.title: Ukraine says underground gas pipeline used to mount sneak attack
item.description:
Ukrainian soldiers spent weeks navigating a decommissioned, underground Soviet-era gas pipeline to sneak behind enemy lines and launch a surprise attack on Russian troops this autumn as part of an operation to prevent the invading forces from reaching the eastern city of Kupiansk, according to the Ukrainian unit involved.
The operation forced the soldiers to get past barricades laid by Russian forces — including the bodies of fallen troops — and involved close-quarters combat inside the roughly three-foot-wide pipeline, Ukraine's military said.
"Operation Veles" was carried out by members of the Ukrainian National Guard's Khartiia Corps in the Kharkiv region within the last couple of months, according to a series of posts by the unit on social media. The unit said troops crawled and were pulled on wheeled carts some nine miles through the underground pipeline before emerging behind Russian positions.
An image from video shared on social media by the Ukrainian National Guard's Khartiia Corps shows a soldier with the unit wincing as he moves through a decommissioned underground gas pipeline north of the front-line city of Kupiansk, as part of "Operation Veles," in the autumn of 2026.
Khartiia Corps/Ukrainian National Guard/Telegram
The operation was part of a broader Ukrainian effort, more than four and a half years into Russia's full-scale invasion, to prevent the invading forces from advancing toward the front-line city of Kupiansk.
The unit's social media posts quoted soldiers saying they engaged in close combat with grenades and small arms inside the pipe, where the cramped space came with pooled freezing water and traces of natural gas lingering years after the pipeline was decommissioned. item.title: Trump in Asia for Putin, Xi summit; possible Kim meeting
item.description:
President Trump arrived Tuesday in the Philippines to start a multiday swing in Asia, where he's scheduled to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and China's President Xi Jinping for a highly anticipated summit later this week.
After landing in Manila, Mr. Trump met with the leaders of the Quad nations that have sought to counter China's influence in the Asia Pacific region, a relationship Mr. Trump described as "very special." Those nations are Australia, India and Japan, as well as the United States.
Mr. Trump announced an $85 million investment in artificial intelligence software, describing it as the "greatest opportunity for economic growth since the Industrial Revolution."
There were protests in Manila ahead of Mr. Trump's trip, with demonstrators holding signs reading "Trump Out," drawings of him as a clown or devil, and signs calling on the public to reject an AI hub named Pax Silica.
Mr. Trump acknowledged that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent have "two lines of thought" on how to handle China, adding that "they handled that very well."
Ahead of his departure from Washington Monday, Mr. Trump called it a "big trip" and said he may also meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in China. After arriving, he said Kim "would like to" come, but "we'll see what happens."
President Trump waves American and Philippine flags after he arrived at Ninoy Aquino International Airport on Nov. 17, 2026, to attend the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit in Manila.
Eloisa Lopez/POOL/AFP via Getty Images

item.title: Pope Leo calls for "less controversy, less war, less division"
item.description:
Rome — Speaking to reporters on his return trip to Rome after an extensive tour of Latin America, Pope Leo XIV called for less political polarization in the United States following the recent midterm elections.
"I would like to see a greater capacity for dialogue, building bridges, reconciliation, less controversy, less war, less division," the Chicago-born leader of the Catholic Church told reporters. "I know this is also a dream, but I know it is possible, so we shall see."
Leo, who confirmed earlier this month that he had voted in the 2026 midterms and was proud to "exercise my right" to do so, said it was the duty of all American citizens to participate in elections. He spoke on the flight back to Italy about his American identity, calling himself "a gringo in many ways."
"My deep faith in democracy, of democratic participation, is also part of being a North American," he said.
Pope Leo XIV speaks to journalists aboard the flight from Lima to Rome, after his Latin American tour, Nov. 16, 2026.
Daniel Dal Zennaro/POOL/AFP/Getty
The pontiff said being American was also likely why he had been forthcoming about his recent health issues.
"Not at 100%, but I'm doing quite well"
"When I speak in general, I am very direct. I say things as they are," he told reporters. "The issue of my health and the fact of openly speaking about it … it's not so typical in many countries and cultures. In U.S. society, it is a bit more of a common attitude."
"I'm not at 100%, but I'm doing quite well," he said, crediting his doctors, prayers and personal determination for his recovery, calling stamina "one of the gifts the Lord gave me."

item.title: Scientist fired after 6-year-old girl dies in gene-editing trial
item.description:
A Chinese scientist who concealed the death of a 6-year-old girl in a gene-editing trial has been fired following a government probe, according to state media.
The girl died last year after receiving experimental gene therapy to correct a non-life-threatening condition — which was not disclosed in published research, an investigation found in July.
Neuroscientist Zilong Qiu, the trial's lead researcher, had made no mention of the girl in a paper published in the prestigious journal Nature, according to the joint investigation by Science and Retraction Watch.
"According to official documents and accounts provided by the girl's parents, the hospital had allowed Qiu's experimental treatment to proceed under a regulatory provision that does not require approval from national regulators," Science reported in July. "After the child's death, the hospital paid a modest fine to a local health authority but Qiu was not publicly sanctioned."
Qiu was dismissed as deputy director of the Songjiang Research Institute affiliated with Shanghai Jiao Tong University, state broadcaster CCTV said Friday, citing a statement from Shanghai authorities.
The reported statement included only Qiu's surname, but referenced the Nature study published on Feb. 18.
Qiu was given a five-year suspension from participating in scientific projects and recorded in a database for "serious breaches of research integrity," the report said.
Another researcher on Qiu's team was fired and handed a five-year suspension, while several others with ties to the hospital where the trial took place were also punished.
The child who died had a rare neurodevelopmental condition called Snijders Blok-Campeau syndrome, according to the report.
The hospital's ethics committee had approved a gene-editing trial to treat the disorder in January 2025, the report said.
The committee terminated the study after the girl died in March due to complications from gene therapy.
